cards.front: What is the value of labelled break in Java?
cards.back: break outer; exits the labelled loop, not just the innermost one
cards.extra: A label prefixes the loop: outer: for(...). It is the only way out of nested loops without a flag variable.

cards.front: Why does (String[]) new Object[]{} throw ClassCastException?
cards.back: The runtime check is on the actual array type, which is Object[] — not on the reference
cards.extra: Casting an array reference does not convert elements. The JVM verifies the component type at the cast.

cards.front: Can a switch match a range like >= 90?
cards.back: No — case labels must be compile-time constants
cards.extra: For ranges use if/else, or divide the score by 10 and switch on that integer.

cards.front: How do you run an external JAR from inside a Java program?
cards.back: new ProcessBuilder("java", "-jar", path).redirectErrorStream(true).start()
cards.extra: Read the merged stream and call waitFor() to get the exit code; without processing the output, the child can block on a full pipe.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::13 JVM and Tooling::03 Core JDK Tools

cards.front: Why is super.super.method() illegal?
cards.back: Java only allows one level up — grandparent access would break encapsulation of the immediate superclass
cards.extra: If you need the grandparent behaviour, that is a design signal: extract it, delegate, or use composition.

cards.front: What causes "class X is public, should be declared in a file named X.java"?
cards.back: A public top-level class whose name does not match its file name
cards.extra: Only non-public classes may share a file. Renaming either the file or the class fixes it.

cards.front: What does getMessage() return for an exception thrown with no message?
cards.back: null — not an empty string
cards.extra: So a null check is needed before logging it; toString() at least includes the class name.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::03 Language Features::01 Exception Handling

cards.front: How do you reliably compare two booleans?
cards.back: Use == on primitives; never equals on boxed values without a null check
cards.extra: Boolean.TRUE.equals(b) is null-safe. b == TRUE compares identity when b is boxed, which the cache only makes safe for the two constants.

cards.front: How do you read the classpath at runtime?
cards.back: System.getProperty("java.class.path") — the ClassLoader API does not expose it
cards.extra: In modular applications that property describes only the unnamed module's path; the module path is not readable this way.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::13 JVM and Tooling::03 Core JDK Tools

cards.front: What is the JavaCompiler API?
cards.back: javax.tools.JavaCompiler from ToolProvider.getSystemJavaCompiler() — compiles source at runtime
cards.extra: You feed it JavaFileObject instances and collect Diagnostic objects, so compilation can happen in memory with no files.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::13 JVM and Tooling::03 Core JDK Tools

cards.front: How do you compile and read source structure programmatically?
cards.back: The Compiler Tree API (com.sun.source.*) exposes the parsed syntax tree and method declarations
cards.extra: That is how tools extract method names, parameters and Javadoc without writing their own parser.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::13 JVM and Tooling::03 Core JDK Tools

cards.front: How do you instantiate an inner class reflectively?
cards.back: Get the constructor that takes the outer instance: Inner.class.getDeclaredConstructor(Outer.class).newInstance(outer)
cards.extra: A non-static inner class has a synthetic first parameter — the enclosing instance — which is easy to miss and throws IllegalArgumentException.

cards.front: How do you read a record's components reflectively?
cards.back: Class.getRecordComponents(), then call each component's accessor
cards.extra: It gives name, type and accessor per component — the clean way to map a record to a map or JSON.

cards.front: Why is Optional a bad record component type?
cards.back: Optional is not Serializable, and it adds a wrapper where a nullable field would do
cards.extra: As a field or parameter type it hides absence behind another layer; Optional is designed for return types.

cards.front: What is the difference between Optional.of and Optional.ofNullable?
cards.back: of(null) throws NullPointerException; ofNullable(null) returns Optional.empty()
cards.extra: Use of when null would be a bug, ofNullable when wrapping an unknown reference.

cards.front: How do you check whether an Optional holds a specific value?
cards.back: optional.filter(v -> v.equals(expected)).isPresent(), or optional.equals(Optional.of(expected))
cards.extra: There is no contains method. filter is clearer and null-safe.

cards.front: How do you replace null with a default value?
cards.back: Optional.ofNullable(x).orElse(default), or Objects.requireNonNullElse(x, default)
cards.extra: The second is shorter and needs no Optional; both handle only the direct null, not nested fields.

cards.front: What is the Elvis operator, and does Java have it?
cards.back: Groovy/Kotlin's ?: — "use this or that". Java has no such operator
cards.extra: The idiom is the ternary x != null ? x : default, or Optional.ofNullable(x).orElse(default).

cards.front: What does yield do in a switch?
cards.back: Returns a value from a block inside a switch expression
cards.extra: case 1 -> { int x = f(); yield x * 2; }. Arrow cases with a single expression need no yield.

cards.front: What are the five uses of the colon in Java?
cards.back:
• Ternary — cond ? a : b
  • Enhanced for — for (T x : xs)
  • Label — outer: before the loop it names
  • switch label — case 1: and default:
  • Assertion detail — assert x > 0 : "msg"
cards.extra: Each form joins two things: ?: separates the true and false branches; the enhanced for joins the loop variable and the Iterable; a label names the statement after it and is the target of break label;; a case or default label ends with a colon; and assert separates the boolean test from the message passed to AssertionError. Note that :: is not a scope-resolution operator in Java — it is the method-reference operator.

cards.front: What makes a variable name illegal for a lambda parameter you do not use?
cards.back: Nothing — Java 21+ allows _ as an unnamed variable
cards.extra: It documents intent: catch (Exception _) says "not used". Unnamed patterns extend this to record deconstruction.

cards.front: What is a compact source file?
cards.back: A single-file program with no class declaration and an instance main — preview in 21, standard in 25
cards.extra: It removes the boilerplate class/static for beginners; the file is implicitly a class and still compiles to normal bytecode.

cards.front: What did JEP 421 do to finalize()?
cards.back: Deprecated it for removal in Java 18, with --finalization=disabled to turn it off
cards.extra: Finalizers can resurrect objects and run unpredictably; the replacement is try-with-resources or Cleaner.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::13 JVM and Tooling::01 JVM Internals

cards.front: What is the difference between readObject and readResolve?
cards.back: readObject customises how an object is read; readResolve replaces the object that deserialization returns
cards.extra: readResolve is how you keep a singleton a singleton across serialization — return the canonical instance.

cards.front: What does a JEP 290 deserialization filter do?
cards.back: Rejects classes during deserialization, either JVM-wide (jdk.serialFilter) or per ObjectInputStream
cards.extra: It is the mitigation for gadget-chain attacks: the filter decides which types may be instantiated before any object is built.

cards.front: What is IncompatibleClassChangeError?
cards.back: A LinkageError thrown when a class's shape changed between compilation and runtime — a class became an interface, or a field became static
cards.extra: Nothing in the source is wrong; the compiled class and the loaded class disagree. Rebuild from clean.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::13 JVM and Tooling::01 JVM Internals

cards.front: What causes UnsatisfiedLinkError?
cards.back: The native library cannot be loaded: wrong architecture, missing dependency, or the wrong file name for System.loadLibrary
cards.extra: On Linux the loader looks for libNAME.so; a mismatch in bitness or libc is the usual culprit.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::13 JVM and Tooling::01 JVM Internals

cards.front: How do you limit how deep the call stack can go?
cards.back: The thread stack size — -Xss — determines when StackOverflowError is thrown
cards.extra: Deep recursion or large frames hit it sooner. Raising it moves the failure, it does not fix the recursion.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::13 JVM and Tooling::01 JVM Internals

cards.front: What does System.out.flush() do that println does not guarantee?
cards.back: Forces buffered output to the underlying stream now
cards.extra: A PrintStream autoflushes on newline only if autoflush was enabled; after a bare print, the text may still sit in the buffer.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::07 IO, Network, Data Formats::01 I-O Operations

cards.front: How do you get the current user's name in Java?
cards.back: System.getProperty("user.name")
cards.extra: It comes from the OS login, so it reflects who started the JVM — not who is using the application.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::13 JVM and Tooling::03 Core JDK Tools

cards.front: How do you clamp a value to a range?
cards.back: Math.clamp(value, min, max) (Java 21), or Math.min(max, Math.max(min, value))
cards.extra: The manual form has existed forever; Math.clamp adds the API and handles the argument ordering for you.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::13 JVM and Tooling::03 Core JDK Tools

cards.front: What is the difference between encapsulation and information hiding?
cards.back: Encapsulation bundles data with behaviour; information hiding restricts access to it
cards.extra: A class can be encapsulated (fields and methods together) and still expose everything. Only hiding protects invariants.

cards.front: Why is static final allowed in either order?
cards.back: Modifier order is not significant: static final and final static compile identically
cards.extra: The JLS defines no preferred order; convention puts static first, and every style guide agrees.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::02 Object Model::04 Static Keyword

cards.front: What is constant folding?
cards.back: A static final constant with a compile-time value is inlined into every user at compile time
cards.extra: Changing the constant then requires recompiling all dependants — the reason constants should be primitive/String and stable.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::02 Object Model::04 Static Keyword

cards.front: Why can an enum not be declared inside an inner class (before Java 16)?
cards.back: An enum is implicitly static, and inner classes could not declare static members
cards.extra: Java 16 relaxed that rule, so the restriction is historical — but the inner class's outer reference is still there for other reasons.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::02 Object Model::05 Nested Classes

cards.front: How do you check whether an object is an enum constant?
cards.back: obj.getClass().isEnum(), or obj instanceof Enum
cards.extra: The first also returns true for a class containing no constants; getClass().getEnumConstants() lists them.

cards.front: What is the recommended naming for interfaces?
cards.back: Adjectives or capability nouns — Runnable, Comparable, List
cards.extra: Java does not use an I prefix; the type reads better in implements clauses without it.

cards.front: What does interface mean versus @interface?
cards.back: interface declares a type; @interface declares an annotation type
cards.extra: An annotation type implicitly extends java.lang.annotation.Annotation, and its methods are annotation elements with optional defaults.

cards.front: What is the difference between Class.cast and the cast operator?
cards.back: Class.cast(obj) is a runtime check that throws a ClassCastException naming the target; the operator is checked by the compiler where possible
cards.extra: Reflection code uses Class.cast because the target type is only known at runtime.

cards.front: How do you mint a random hexadecimal string?
cards.back: Generate bytes with SecureRandom and hex-encode them
cards.extra: String.format("%08x", random.nextInt()) works for an 8-digit value, but SecureRandom is what you want for tokens.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::13 JVM and Tooling::03 Core JDK Tools

cards.front: How do you create an object without running a constructor?
cards.back: With Objenesis or Unsafe/ReflectionFactory allocation — the frameworks' trick
cards.extra: Mocking and deserialization libraries need instances whose constructor would fail or have side effects.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::02 Object Model::01 Classes and Objects

cards.front: How do you get a generic type's Class at runtime?
cards.back: Pass a Class<T> token into the constructor, or read ParameterizedType from a subclass's getGenericSuperclass()
cards.extra: Erasure removes the argument from the class itself; only signatures and explicit tokens keep it.

cards.front: What -Xlint category flags raw types?
cards.back: -Xlint:rawtypes — plus -Xlint:unchecked for unchecked conversions
cards.extra: Raw type warnings are off by default, which is why they spread unnoticed in older codebases.

cards.front: What are value-based classes?
cards.back: Classes the JDK says to treat as values — Integer, Optional, LocalDate — where identity is unspecified
cards.extra: They may be freely reused or cached, so ==, synchronized on them and identityHashCode are incorrect.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::02 Object Model::01 Classes and Objects

cards.front: What is the Vector API?
cards.back: An incubator API for SIMD vector computation, expressing operations that map to CPU vector instructions
cards.extra: It is not standard yet; the JVM chooses the best instruction set at runtime.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::13 JVM and Tooling::03 Core JDK Tools

cards.front: How do you avoid a method with ten parameters?
cards.back: Introduce a parameter object or a builder
cards.extra: The signature stops being readable and every call site must know the order; grouping related parameters fixes both.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::02 Object Model::02 Attributes and Methods

cards.front: How do you run a method only once, safely?
cards.back: AtomicBoolean.compareAndSet, a CountDownLatch, or the holder-class idiom for static init
cards.extra: A plain boolean flag is racy; these give exactly-once semantics under concurrency.
